instructions:
## Research objective

Your goal is to design reasoning and prompt engineering techniques to maximize accuracy for measuring, simulating, and mitigating AI’s impacts on the future of work (labor displacement, shared prosperity, learning harms, detectability, and copyright compensation).

## Plan Formulation

- Operationalize the paper’s six propositions (P1–P6) into measurable hypotheses and evaluation modules: A) Labor-market shocks and technical-debt externalities; B) Pace and distributional effects of automation; C) Shared prosperity and bargaining power; D) Uneven democratization across countries; E) Learning harms and content homogenization; F) Detectability/watermarking and copyright compensation mechanisms.
- Pre-register a high-level analysis plan delineating primary outcomes, secondary outcomes, window definitions, and robustness checks for Modules A–F. Record all assumptions and potential confounders (platform mix shifts, seasonality, macro shocks, policy changes).
- Restrict to license-clean data and transparent methods; avoid scraping in violation of terms of service; prioritize open APIs and archival sources (e.g., OpenAlex, World Bank, OII Online Labour Index, Internet Archive).
- Use LLMs for: data cleaning, coding assistance, taxonomy mapping, qualitative coding of job categories, and prompt-based labeling. Do not use LLM outputs as “human writing” baselines; collect human data with consent when needed.
- Select evaluation windows anchored to major product releases: Stable Diffusion (2022-08), ChatGPT (2022-11), and subsequent model milestones (document dates). Use staggered-adoption DiD and event studies where applicable.
- Define policy-simulation scenarios aligned to recommendations R1–R6 (worker support, open AI, detection/watermarking, royalty mechanisms, anti-capture governance).
- Risk management: obtain IRB or equivalent ethics approval for studies with human participants; minimize personal data; anonymize and aggregate; document model limits and false-positive risks in detection studies.

## Data Preparation

- Module A (Labor-market shocks):
-   - Source job postings and task mix time series from the Oxford Internet Institute Online Labour Index (OLI) and other open releases; supplement with platform public dashboards and the Internet Archive for category snapshots, respecting TOS.
-   - Map categories into “automation-prone” vs “manual-intensive” (e.g., writing, coding, image creation vs delivery, manual services) via a transparent taxonomy. Use LLM-assisted labeling with human verification on a stratified sample.
-   - Construct an event dataset with monthly counts per category, geography (if available), and platform, 12–24 months pre-event and 18–24 months post-event. Include macro controls (e.g., OECD unemployment, CPI).
- Module B (Automation distributional effects):
-   - Assemble open benchmarks of coding and content tasks (e.g., HumanEval variants, Codeforces practice, open-ended writing prompts). Partition tasks by skill level.
-   - If no human-subjects study is feasible, run simulated assistance conditions: none, tool-assist (autocomplete, search), LLM-co-pilot (model-in-the-loop). Record latency, quality scores, and error profiles. Clearly caveat generalizability.
- Module C (Shared prosperity and bargaining power):
-   - Compile national/regional indicators: wage growth by decile (World Bank, OECD), union density, collective bargaining coverage, and capital vs labor income shares (WIID/WID), 2016–2025.
-   - Construct firm-concentration proxies in AI (e.g., share of AI patents, compute spend signals, cloud region presence) using OpenAlex, patent datasets, and cloud provider public region lists.
- Module D (Uneven democratization):
-   - Build a country-level “AI Capacity Index”: normalized z-scores over compute access proxies (cloud regions, data centers), AI publications (OpenAlex), data governance maturity (GDPR-like legal indices), digitization levels (World Bank).
-   - Build a “Data Colonialism Risk Index”: normalized exposure to imported AI, dataset scarcity, and weak data protection. Document design choices.
- Module E (Learning harms, homogenization):
-   - Collect human-written texts: consented essays from crowd platforms (Prolific/MTurk) with fair pay and explicit consent; or use open corpora resembling essays/creative writing (e.g., Reddit WritingPrompts via Pushshift under TOS).
-   - Generate LLM-written counterparts using multiple models (open-weight where possible): Llama 3 8B/70B, Mixtral 8x7B, and one compact commercial model. Record temperatures, seeds, and system prompts.
-   - For math/problem-solving, create practice sets (e.g., open-source algebra/calculus items) with pre/post tests; if running a human study, collect baseline ability and retention after delay. Otherwise, restrict to content-diversity analyses.
- Module F (Detectability, watermarking, copyright compensation):
-   - Detectors: clone and set up open detectors (e.g., Binoculars) and any accessible research baselines; document API detectors (e.g., Checkfor.ai, GPTZero) if terms allow. Build a balanced dataset: Human, LLM-zero-shot, LLM-paraphrased, LLM-translated, and LLM-fine-tuned outputs.
-   - Watermarking: implement a greenlist-based text watermark (e.g., “A Watermark for LLMs”-style), log watermark strength, and test robustness under paraphrase, translation, and summarization.
-   - Copyright compensation simulation: construct a license-clean training pool (Project Gutenberg authors with clear PD status, CC-BY Wikipedia, CC News). Fine-tune small LMs on author-partitioned corpora; apply Monte Carlo Shapley approximations to estimate contribution scores (SRS) for generated outputs. Do not use copyrighted or disputed datasets (e.g., Books3, LibGen).

## Running Experiments

- Environment: Python 3.11; pin packages (pandas, numpy, statsmodels, linearmodels, scikit-learn, spacy, textstat, epitran/langid for language ID, gensim, scipy, matplotlib/seaborn, geopandas for maps, openalexapi, huggingface datasets/transformers, accelerate, peft, bitsandbytes). Containerize with a lockfile for reproducibility.
- Common LLM usage policy: use LLMs for labeling/coding assistance with clear instructions to output JSON only; set deterministic decoding (temperature=0) for classification; never mix LLM-generated text into the “human” class.
- Module A (DiD/event study):
-   - Fit two-way fixed effects models with platform and month FE; use treatment indicators for automation-prone categories post-event; include event-study leads/lags to test pre-trends.
-   - Run placebo events and alternative cutoffs (±1–2 months); reweight by platform share; cluster SEs at category or platform level; visualize dynamic treatment effects.
- Module B (Automation—performance distribution):
-   - For simulated assistance: run tasks with three conditions (None, Tool, LLM-CoPilot). For code tasks, measure correctness (unit tests) and time-to-solve; for writing, use blinded rubric scoring (grammar, coherence, originality) by human raters.
-   - Estimate heterogeneous effects by task complexity; assess whether assistance disproportionately boosts higher-skilled tasks, consistent with P2.
- Module C (Shared prosperity):
-   - Build panel regressions linking AI concentration proxies to changes in wage shares and union density, controlling for GDP growth, sector mix, and policy dummies; test IVs or lag structures when available.
- Module D (Global uneven democratization):
-   - Standardize indicators to z-scores and compute composite indices with PCA and equal-weighted variants; correlate AI Capacity Index with exposure to AI-driven task displacement (from Felten et al.-style occupation exposure scores if accessible).
-   - Produce choropleth maps; run quantile regressions to see where gaps are largest.
- Module E (Learning harms and homogenization):
-   - Compute diversity metrics: type-token ratio, MTLD, unique n-gram rates, syntactic variety (POS tag entropy), and topic entropy. Compute Jensen–Shannon divergence across author/model clusters.
-   - Homogenization test: compare dispersion in stylistic feature space between human and LLM corpora; test whether LLM assistance reduces variance across prompts (algorithmic monoculture signal).
-   - If running human learning study: randomized assignment to practice-with-LLM vs control; measure immediate performance and delayed retention; analyze with ANCOVA controlling for baseline.
- Module F (Detectability and watermarking):
-   - Build evaluation sets: 2k–5k samples stratified by genre, length, and language; include paraphrase (back-translation), translation, and summarization attacks. Report ROC-AUC, precision@fixed FPR (e.g., 1%), and confusion matrices.
-   - For fine-tuned text generation, fine-tune an open model on in-domain style data (license-clean) to test detector limits. Do not publish evasion recipes; aggregate results responsibly.
-   - Watermark experiments: vary watermark strength; measure detection under editing perturbations; assess utility loss (fluency, perplexity).
-   - SRS simulation: approximate Shapley values with permutation sampling (e.g., k=100–500 permutations per prompt); compare SRS allocations under alternative similarity-based proxies to bound compute.
- Governance/policy simulations:
-   - Worker-support counterfactuals: microsimulate the effect of retraining stipends or wage insurance on displaced worker cohorts using stylized assumptions; perform sensitivity analysis.
-   - Open vs closed data regimes: scenario analysis for concentration metrics and innovation entry under alternative governance assumptions (R2, R6).
- Reproducibility: maintain a run registry (W&B or MLflow), log seeds, data hashes, model versions, and prompts; export all figures with metadata.

## Results Interpretation

- Module A: A significant post-event decline in automation-prone postings (relative to controls) supports P1; inspect dynamic effects, platform heterogeneity, and robustness to alternative windows. Discuss technical-debt externalities if instability or category redefinitions coincide with rapid model releases.
- Module B: If assistance benefits accrue more to complex tasks or high-skill proxies, interpret as acceleration of skill disparity (P2). Caveat limitations of simulated settings.
- Module C: Positive association between AI concentration and declining labor share/union density supports P3; probe causality carefully (lags, IVs), and report nulls transparently.
- Module D: Large cross-country variance in AI Capacity Index with high Data Colonialism Risk in low-income contexts supports P4. Discuss data governance gaps and dependency channels.
- Module E: Reduced stylistic dispersion or content diversity in LLM outputs vs human baselines supports homogenization claims; if human-with-LLM texts converge toward model style, emphasize risks for education/creativity (P5). If learning studies show worse retention with assistance, align with Bastani et al.-style findings.
- Module F: Detector performance degradation under fine-tuning/paraphrase quantifies current limits; robust watermarks with acceptable utility cost support R4 feasibility; SRS simulations showing stable, interpretable allocations bolster R5’s viability. Carefully report false-positive risks and ethical implications.
- Cross-cutting: Triangulate evidence across modules; do not overgeneralize platform-specific effects; highlight where results counter the paper’s positions, and identify boundary conditions.

## Report Writing

- Provide an executive summary mapping findings to P1–P6 and recommendations R1–R6, stating which claims are supported, mixed, or not supported, with effect sizes and uncertainty.
- Detail datasets, licenses, and data provenance; include a data sheet/model card and an ethics statement (IRB status, participant compensation, privacy safeguards).
- Document all prompts, model versions, and decoding settings used for labeling and generation; publish few-shot templates and classification schemas.
- Include visualizations: event-study coefficient plots; choropleth maps for indices; diversity dispersion plots; ROC curves for detectors; watermark robustness curves; Shapley allocation distributions.
- Provide robustness and sensitivity appendices, including alternative specifications, placebo tests, and ablations (e.g., different index weightings).
- Release code and configuration files (container, lockfile, run registry), with redactions for any content that could reasonably facilitate detector evasion; adhere to reproducible science best practices.
- Discuss policy implications and trade-offs, emphasizing worker support mechanisms, governance against regulatory capture, and the practicality of collective licensing and watermark mandates.
